requirements.requirement: Forward inventory-tagged log messages from node2 to node1 and persist them at /var/log/inventory/node2.log.
requirements.summary: A live inventory-tagged marker emitted on node2 was observed in the required node1 file. Final evidence shows four records received across the test period and the collector/sender configurations remained valid and active.

requirements.requirement: Keep log forwarding and persisted data working after either node1 or node2 restarts.
requirements.summary: Both nodes had healthy pre-restart states, acknowledged restarts, changed boot IDs, and recovered rsyslog state. Following node1's restart, a newly emitted record was received; following node2's restart, another newly emitted record was received. Earlier records remained present.

requirements.requirement: Retain the installed operating-system release and kernel and use compatible logging software.
requirements.summary: Both nodes remained on CentOS Stream 10 with kernel 6.12.0-205.el10.x86_64 before and after execution. The existing platform rsyslog package was used, its configurations validated, and its service operated successfully through both restarts.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied. Direct tests demonstrate inventory-tagged delivery to the required file, persistence and renewed delivery after each node restart, complete provider-wide restart evidence for both managed nodes, and retention of the original OS and kernel.
limitations: The claimed message sent “during” node1's restart was emitted before the reboot actually began: node1 still showed its old boot ID afterward. It therefore does not prove queueing during collector downtime, although a separate fresh message was directly delivered after node1 completed its restart.
No real inventory application service or pre-existing application logs were observed; forwarding behavior was validated using synthetic logger messages carrying the inventory identifier.

operational_hygiene.summary: Configuration files, service restarts, test messages, firewall changes, and node restarts all had clear roles in implementation or bounded verification. No abandoned files, failed services, or package damage were observed. One retained hygiene concern is that TCP/514 was opened permanently to the entire active firewall zone and rsyslog listens on all IPv4/IPv6 interfaces, although only node2 needed access; this exposure is broader than necessary. No other unnecessary mutations were identified.
